title: BootForge drill bank: everyday JS, React, SQL and TS
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 bank-bootforge row). Scope = the 16 BootForge courses; archived units under them are skipped by the reader. Sources and siblings are live drills of the lessons that teach the idea. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Reshape arrays and objects by building new ones (spread, map, filter, slice) and copy every level you change; leave the input untouched.
ideas.why: Mutating an input you were handed changes it for every other holder of the reference, which shows up as stale screens and flaky tests far from the edit.
ideas.prompt: `function addTag(user, tag) { user.profile.tags.push(tag); return { ...user }; }` returns a new object, yet the caller's original user also gains the tag. Why, and what is the correct version?
ideas.answer: The spread copies only the top level: profile and its tags array are still the same objects, and push changed them in place. Copy each level on the path you change: a new user with a new profile holding a new array that contains the old tags plus the new one.

ideas.idea: Run independent async work in parallel and dependent work in order, and decide on purpose what one rejection does to the rest.
ideas.why: Awaiting independent calls one by one wastes time, and an unhandled rejection either crashes the process or silently drops the other results.
ideas.prompt: A dashboard loads a user, then that user's orders, and also the store's opening hours, which nothing depends on. Each step is awaited in turn, and one failing call blanks the whole page. Restructure it.
ideas.answer: Orders need the user, so those two stay in order; the opening hours do not, so start them at the same time as the user. Wait for both groups together, and handle failures per piece (a result object or allSettled), so a failed opening-hours call shows a placeholder instead of hiding the orders.

ideas.idea: Write every Express handler in the same order: validate the input, do the work, then send the status that says what happened (201, 204, 400, 404).
ideas.why: Handlers that act before validating corrupt data, and ones that always answer 200 leave clients unable to tell success from failure.
ideas.prompt: POST /tasks writes to the store first, then checks that title is non-empty and, if it is not, answers with a success status and an error text. Rewrite the handler's flow and statuses.
ideas.answer: Check the body first and return 400 with the field and reason if title is missing, before touching the store. Create the task only after validation and answer 201 with it. Map a missing parent or id to 404, and make sure each path returns once, so no later line sends a second response.

ideas.idea: Keep the smallest state that can describe the screen and compute everything else during render; never store a value you can derive.
ideas.why: A second copy of derived data falls out of sync the first time someone updates one and forgets the other.
ideas.prompt: A todo component keeps `todos` and also `doneCount` in state, updating both in each handler. After a bulk edit the counter shows the wrong number. What is the design fix?
ideas.answer: doneCount is a function of todos, so it should not be state at all. Compute it on render, todos.filter(t => t.done).length, or with a selector, and delete the second setState from every handler. One source of truth cannot disagree with itself.

ideas.idea: When two components need the same state, move it to their closest common parent and pass value and callbacks down; when its updates multiply, use a reducer.
ideas.why: Two components each holding their own copy drift apart, and update logic scattered over handlers is hard to test and easy to break.
ideas.prompt: A Celsius input and a Fahrenheit input each keep their own state and try to sync with effects. Typing fast makes them disagree. Later, a cart has six handlers that each update items. How do you structure both?
ideas.answer: Keep one temperature in the parent, derive both displays from it, and pass each input its value and an onChange that updates the parent; no syncing effects. For the cart, move every update into one reducer with named actions, so the logic is a pure function you can test with an action log.

ideas.idea: SQL works in a fixed order: FROM and JOIN build rows, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY makes groups, HAVING filters groups, then ORDER BY sorts.
ideas.why: Filtering an aggregate in WHERE fails, filtering rows in HAVING is slow and confusing, and an inner join silently drops rows with no match.
ideas.prompt: You need customers who spent more than 500 on paid orders, including the total, biggest spenders first. A teammate writes `WHERE SUM(total) > 500`. Explain why it fails and write the clause order you would use.
ideas.answer: WHERE runs before grouping, so no sum exists yet. Join customers to orders, keep only paid orders in WHERE, group by customer, keep groups whose summed total exceeds 500 in HAVING, then order by that sum descending. Use a LEFT JOIN only when customers with no orders must appear.

ideas.idea: Start a TypeScript function from its signature: parameter types, return type and the failure cases, then write the body to satisfy it.
ideas.why: Bodies written first produce inferred types that leak implementation details, and callers find the mismatch only at runtime.
ideas.prompt: A helper `parseQuantity(input)` sometimes returns a number, sometimes NaN and sometimes throws. Callers keep adding their own checks. What signature would you write first, and what does it force?
ideas.answer: Decide the contract before the body, for example `parseQuantity(input: string): number | null`, with null meaning 'not a valid quantity' and no throwing. The return type makes every caller handle the null case, the compiler checks the body against it, and the helper's behaviour is visible without reading it.
